title: Create a meal that feels like part of your wedding
focus: Start with the atmosphere you want guests to experience and the food that matters to you as a couple. A plated dinner, generous sharing menu and lively station service each have a different rhythm. Review the venue, speeches and other programme moments before finalising the courses. A tasting can help refine dishes and presentation where arranged, while the written proposal defines the actual service. Include dietary requirements and the complete guest count so the plan is thoughtful for every table.

sections.title: Plan the wedding meal from arrival to the final course
paragraphs: Begin with the moments around the meal: guest arrival, the ceremony, photographs, speeches and the first dance. A canapé reception can cover the welcome period before everyone sits down. A buffet or live station creates a different pace, so allow time for guests to move and return to their tables comfortably.

Wedding menu planning should include the complete guest list, children’s meals, dietary alternatives and any food that has personal or cultural importance. Decide whether the meal is plated, shared or served from stations before finalising individual dishes. A tasting, where arranged, helps refine flavour and presentation; its scope and cost should be confirmed separately.

Check the venue’s catering access, kitchen facilities, equipment rules and service deadline. Agree who receives and stores an externally supplied cake and who coordinates changes to the programme. Use the wedding catering checklist to bring these details together before approving the final menu, staffing and equipment.

sections.title: Give the menu a clear direction
paragraphs: Plan the welcome food and the main wedding meal together. Tell us whether guests will have canapés before sitting down, visit a buffet or receive a plated menu. The reception length, ceremony timing and venue kitchen affect how those stages can fit together.

Create one guest list that records dietary requirements and the arrangements for children, suppliers or other people who need a meal. Agree how alternatives will be identified with your venue or planner, including who holds the final version of the list.

Use the tasting discussion to assess the actual proposed dishes and presentation. Confirm any tasting fee, menu changes and final-number deadlines in writing, then check that service staff, crockery, equipment and clearance are covered in the event proposal.

sections.title: Build the service schedule around your guests
paragraphs: Work backwards from the time guests should begin eating. The team may need access earlier for unloading, setup and preparation, particularly when equipment or several service areas are involved. Share the programme before the menu is finalised so the catering plan can support it.

Identify moments when service should pause, such as a speech, presentation or ceremony. For an office event, confirm the length of each break and whether everyone will arrive at once. For a private celebration, allow for the welcome period and any cake or toast that needs its own place in the sequence.

Agree a contact for changes on the day. Small timing adjustments may be manageable, while a substantial extension can affect staffing and the booked hours. Clear communication helps the team respond sensibly and keeps the food connected to the occasion rather than running on a separate timetable.
